hbm.intro:
HBM (High Bandwidth Memory) is memory assembled into a vertical stack of thin DRAM dies and mounted on a shared substrate right up against the processor. The binding constraint on a large AI model is not arithmetic speed but the rate at which data arrives: ordinary memory hangs off a narrow bus, centimetres of board traces away, and the processor idles waiting. HBM removes that constraint — data travels over thousands of parallel lines across millimetres, and a single stack delivers more than a terabyte per second. That is why an AI accelerator cannot do without HBM.

How it works. Ordinary DRAM dies are first thinned for this: the wafer is ground from the back from roughly 780 down to 30–50 microns, or a tall stack will not fit the package height and will shed heat badly. Thousands of micro-holes are then etched all the way through each thinned die and filled with copper — these are the through-silicon vias (TSVs), vertical wires connecting every layer at once. Then 8, 12 or 16 dies are stacked and bonded: either through micro solder bumps between layers (thermocompression), or, from 16-layer HBM4 onward, copper directly to copper with no gap (hybrid bonding). The stack sits on top of a bottom logic die (the base die), which runs the whole memory and talks to the processor. The finished stack is mounted on a silicon interposer beside the processor, putting memory and processor in one package.

The hard, expensive part here is not the memory cells but assembling the stack without defects and getting the heat out. At 12–16 layers with thousands of connections, one bad die or one unbonded joint kills the entire stack, taking every good layer beneath it with it. The taller the stack, the more tightly hot dies are packed and the harder it is to pull heat out of the middle, so thinning and the bonding method decide directly how many stacks come out good. The spread in stack yield is the main hidden profit lever: Samsung's HBM4 memory yielded only around 50% in early 2026 (nearly every second die scrapped), whereas the leader's proven bonding process loses markedly less. Whoever assembles with fewer defects takes the margin.

Who pays, and how much. HBM is the most expensive part of an accelerator: a single chip carries 6–8 stacks, and memory accounts for roughly 63% of the cost of a finished AI chip, against only ~13% for the compute die itself (Epoch AI). One HBM4 stack costs ~$500–550, meaning $3–4K of memory in every accelerator; each generation costs more — from ~$200 (HBM3) to $300 (HBM3E) and $500+ (HBM4). Buyers pay without haggling, because without HBM the accelerator simply does not work and the delivery queue is booked years out: cloud giants and accelerator makers prepay to reserve capacity — Micron alone holds ~$22B of customer prepayments and ~$100B of contracted future revenue. The makers, in turn, are putting tens of billions into expansion: SK Hynix has up to $75B of capex through 2028, roughly 80% of it in HBM.

Three makers hold the market: SK Hynix ~56%, Samsung and Micron at roughly ~21% each. The segment itself grows from ~$35B (2025) to ~$100B (2028) on Micron's estimate — faster than any other part of memory; demand added +130% in 2025 and another ~70% in 2026.

One term that recurs below: a «node» (process technology), such as 3 nm or 2 nm, is a generation of chip manufacturing technology. The nanometre figure is a nominal label for transistor size: the smaller it is, the finer and denser the transistors and the faster and more efficient the chip — but the harder and costlier the node is to master. Only TSMC, Samsung and Intel can run leading-edge nodes (3 nm and below); «mature» nodes (28–45 nm and older) are commodity technology, cheap and widely available.
hbm.thesis.bigIdea: The market prices HBM as ordinary cyclical memory about to collapse. But HBM has quietly decoupled from the commodity cycle: it is sold out years ahead on prepaid contracts with price floors, and its real constraint is not wafers but defect-free assembly yield. So both the high price and the record margin last longer than the market assumes — and the yield leader (SK Hynix) keeps extending its lead.
hbm.thesis.stream.0.t: Where the money in an AI chip actually sits
hbm.thesis.stream.1.t: An investor buying «Nvidia's suppliers» thinks they are buying compute. In fact they are buying memory. In the cost of a modern AI chip, 63% is HBM memory and only about 13% is the compute die itself. Over the past two years the value quietly moved from logic to memory: every accelerator carries 6–8 HBM modules worth $3–4K — more than the processor.

hbm.thesis.stream.12.t: When a customer puts down $22B of prepayments and fixes a price floor two years out, this is no longer an exchange-traded commodity but infrastructure designed into the project. That is what first partly decoupled HBM from the classic memory cycle.
hbm.thesis.stream.13.t: The real constraint is not wafers, it is scrap
hbm.thesis.stream.14.t: And it is not the wafers that cap output. The cap is final stack assembly: fine-drilling the channels through the layers, the queue for bonding machines and — above all — how many assembled stacks come out defect-free. Whoever assembles with fewer defects takes the margin.
hbm.thesis.stream.15.items.0.n: nearly every second die scrapped — which is why Samsung trails on margin
hbm.thesis.stream.15.items.1.n: thanks to its proprietary layer-bonding method; and it sheds heat better
hbm.thesis.stream.16.t: This is why SK Hynix leads — not on wafers, but on yield. And the advantage compounds: less scrap → lower unit cost → more margin to invest in the next generation's lead.
hbm.thesis.stream.17.label: HOW TO BUY THE CONSTRAINT ITSELF
hbm.thesis.stream.17.t: The pure play on the shortage is not memory but the layer-bonding machines: Hanmi and Besi. Their equipment is needed however the share split among the three makers lands.
hbm.thesis.stream.19.t: There are only three makers, and a single Nvidia order moves all of their shares at once.

hbm.thesis.stream.21.t: What is already priced in — and where the anomaly is
hbm.thesis.stream.22.t: And here is the anomaly. A record 72% operating margin, years of prepaid backlog — and SK Hynix trades at 5–8x earnings, Micron at about 12x. A low multiple on a record margin is not cheapness, it is the market betting on an imminent profit fall. The market is pricing a cycle peak, not a growing business.
hbm.thesis.stream.23.items.0.n: memory at a peak usually trades at 8–12x — this is cheaper still
hbm.thesis.stream.23.items.1.n: the cheapest way in, and the only way to buy HBM on a US exchange
hbm.thesis.stream.23.items.2.n: a record — and precisely what the market thinks cannot hold
hbm.thesis.stream.24.t: Our read: the argument is not about direction but about duration. Contract price floors, $22B of prepayments and the barrier of Nvidia qualification stretch the peak out. If the shortage holds through 2027 (and SK Hynix's chief says beyond 2030), then 5–8x is far too cheap. The market is looking at a quarter; we are looking at two contract cycles.
hbm.thesis.stream.26.t: The thesis rests on the shortage. Three signals would say it is over — and it is worth remembering that from 2027 growth rests increasingly on price, and price is the first thing to break when supply catches up:

hbm.thesis.stream.27.rows.1.0: New fabs from all three + China's CXMT passes qualification (2028)
hbm.thesis.stream.27.rows.1.1: Supply catches demand — the shortage ends
hbm.thesis.stream.27.rows.2.1: The price floor the thesis stands on stops holding
hbm.thesis.stream.28.t: None of them is lit yet: contracts keep reaching further out, and Samsung has not closed the yield gap.
hbm.thesis.stream.29.t: The bottom line — if you remember one thing
hbm.thesis.stream.3.t: What HBM is, and why nothing works without it
hbm.thesis.stream.30.t: HBM triples to ~$100B by 2028, and it is paid for by the data centres of giants who have the money. Memory has quietly become the most expensive and the most heavily contracted part of an AI chip — and the market still prices it as a commodity on the edge of a crash.
hbm.thesis.stream.31.t: Compressed into one thought: the market is pricing a collapse, and the contracts say otherwise. The best-protected ways to buy it are the yield leader (SK Hynix) and the only maker available on a US exchange (Micron), for as long as the shortage holds, plus the bonding machines (Hanmi/Besi), which are needed however the shares fall. Samsung is a separate bet on a comeback and a share shift.
hbm.thesis.stream.4.t: HBM is several ordinary memory dies stacked on top of one another and threaded with vertical channels through the silicon (TSVs), so data travels up and down rather than around. The finished stack sits right against the compute chip on a shared substrate. Without it the accelerator «starves»: the compute core idles waiting for data. Each generation costs more than the last: $200 (HBM3) → $300 (HBM3E) → $500+ (HBM4).
hbm.thesis.stream.5.t: What the market thinks: «it's memory, it will crash»
hbm.thesis.stream.6.t: Memory has always been a brutal commodity cycle: boom → fab build-out → glut → price collapse. The market prices HBM by the same reflex. In July 2026 the makers' shares fell more than 20% — on record results. Everyone knows memory is cyclical, and everyone rushes to price the peak first.
hbm.thesis.stream.7.items.0.l: earnings is what SK Hynix costs
hbm.thesis.stream.7.items.0.n: on a record 72% operating margin — the market is pricing a profit fall, not growth
hbm.thesis.stream.7.items.1.n: on a record quarter — the classic «this is the cycle peak» reaction
hbm.thesis.stream.8.t: Why HBM decoupled from the cycle
hbm.thesis.stream.9.t: But HBM is not traded on an exchange at a spot price the way ordinary memory is. It is contracted years ahead, prepaid, with a price floor, and co-designed with the customer. Commodities do not behave like that.
hbm.tldr.0: The best supply/demand set-up memory has seen in 40 years: three makers share the market (SK Hynix 56%, Samsung ~21%, Micron ~21%), all of 2026 is sold out, and the market goes from ~$35B (2025) to ~$100B (2028), growing ~40% a year.
hbm.tldr.1: The best return-for-risk is SK Hynix (the leader: ~70% of HBM4 supply — the newest generation of this stacked memory — is reserved for Vera Rubin, Nvidia's next accelerator generation, on a 72% operating margin). Micron is the cheapest way in (forward P/E ~12). Hanmi / Besi / TSMC supply the equipment and the final assembly for this link.
hbm.tldr.2: The main risk is cyclicality: memory gets cheaper the moment supply catches demand, and by 2027–2028 all three makers will have finished new fabs. The sector already fell >20% in July 2026. The question is whether multi-year contracts and prepayments hold the price when that new supply arrives.
hbm.verdict.bear.0: Oversupply in 2028: the new fabs together (three makers plus China's CXMT) outrun demand growth, and analysts start talking about a «market correction».
hbm.verdict.bear.1: China (CXMT — a new Chinese memory maker) breaks the trio's market: its memory passes qualification at a Western giant, its defect-free share rises, and it completes an $8.55B IPO.
hbm.verdict.bear.2: The ordinary memory cycle returns: spot prices turn down, inventories build, and margins come off the 85–92% peak.
hbm.verdict.bull.0: The shortage holds to 2028: on the Q3–Q4 2026 calls the makers say «sold out» again, and final chip assembly at TSMC stays short.
hbm.verdict.bull.1: HBM (stacked memory) prices rise several-fold in 2027: visible in contract pricing (TrendForce data) and in the average selling prices the makers disclose in H2 2026.
hbm.verdict.bull.2: HBM profits have decoupled from the old memory cycle: contracted commitments and prepayments keep growing (~$100B at Micron), and the price floors written into contracts hold.
hbm.verdict.horizon: about 2 years — the window of HBM shortage and high prices (2026–2027); by 2027–2028 new fabs catch demand and the cycle turns down.
hbm.verdict.keyQuestion: Will HBM demand absorb the 2027–2028 fabs — or will overbuild collapse prices the way it did in 2018 and 2022?
hbm.verdict.summary: A strong structural story: memory is acutely short, only three companies make it, and demand is contracted years ahead — hence the record prices and margins. But memory carries a built-in risk: by 2027–2028 all three makers (plus the Chinese newcomer CXMT) will have finished new fabs. When that supply arrives and catches demand, memory prices fall and profits with them — that is how every previous cycle ended. Hence a 7, not a 9.
hbm.whatIsIt: Memory assembled into a vertical stack of thin dies and placed right up against the compute chip. A large AI model sits idle not for lack of arithmetic speed but because ordinary memory cannot feed it data fast enough; this stack feeds it through a far wider pipe over a very short distance. That is why an AI accelerator cannot do without it — it is the most expensive and the scarcest part of the chip.
